claim: Simple individual-level behavioral rules can give rise to emergent group-level behavior in complex biological systems.
source: In complex biological systems, simple individual-level behavioral rules can give rise to emergent group-level behavior.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that frames the study's conceptual foundation.

claim: Collective behavior has been well studied in cells and larger organisms.
source: While collective behavior has been well studied in cells and larger organisms, the mesoscopic scale is less understood, as it is unclear which sensory inputs and physical processes matter a priori.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The mesoscopic scale of collective behavior is less understood because it is unclear which sensory inputs and physical processes matter a priori.
source: While collective behavior has been well studied in cells and larger organisms, the mesoscopic scale is less understood, as it is unclear which sensory inputs and physical processes matter a priori.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: C. elegans exhibits both aggregation and swarming behaviors during collective feeding.
source: Here, we investigate collective feeding in the roundworm C. elegans at this intermediate scale, using quantitative phenotyping and agent-based modeling to identify behavioral rules underlying both aggregation and swarming—a dynamic phenotype only observed at longer timescales.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental observations described throughout the manuscript.

claim: Swarming in C. elegans is a dynamic phenotype only observed at longer timescales.
source: Here, we investigate collective feeding in the roundworm C. elegans at this intermediate scale, using quantitative phenotyping and agent-based modeling to identify behavioral rules underlying both aggregation and swarming—a dynamic phenotype only observed at longer timescales.
evidence: This is based on the temporal observations reported in the study.

claim: Three key behavioral rules underlie C. elegans aggregation: cluster-edge reversals, a density-dependent switch between crawling speeds, and taxis towards neighboring worms.
source: Then we use agent-based simulations and approximate Bayesian inference to identify three key behavioral rules for aggregation: cluster-edge reversals, a density-dependent switch between crawling speeds, and taxis towards neighboring worms.
evidence: This claim is supported by the agent-based modeling and Bayesian inference results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Swarming is driven by local food depletion but employs the same behavioral mechanisms as initial aggregation.
source: Our simulations suggest that swarming is simply driven by local food depletion but otherwise employs the same behavioral mechanisms as the initial aggregation.
evidence: This is based on simulation results with food depletion models.

claim: Alignment is important for flocking behavior in both theoretical models and birds.
source: While very different in their details, shared principles have begun to emerge, such as the importance of alignment for flocking behavior in both theoretical models and birds (Bialek et al., 2012; Pearce et al., 2014; Reynolds, 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Collective behavior at the microscale is controlled by molecule diffusion and direct contact between cells or particles.
source: Until now, the study of collective behavior has mainly focused on cells and active particles at the microscale, controlled by molecule diffusion and direct contact between cells or particles (Köhler et al., 2011; De Palo et al., 2017; Peruani et al., 2012; Starruß et al., 2012), and on animals at the macroscale, aided by long-range visual cues (Bialek et al., 2012; Katz et al., 2011; Pearce et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Collective behavior at the macroscale is aided by long-range visual cues.
source: Until now, the study of collective behavior has mainly focused on cells and active particles at the microscale, controlled by molecule diffusion and direct contact between cells or particles (Köhler et al., 2011; De Palo et al., 2017; Peruani et al., 2012; Starruß et al., 2012), and on animals at the macroscale, aided by long-range visual cues (Bialek et al., 2012; Katz et al., 2011; Pearce et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: C. elegans is 1 mm long.
source: C. elegans collective behavior can contribute to bridging this scale gap. Some strains of this 1 mm-long roundworm are known to aggregate into groups on food (de Bono and Bargmann, 1998); here we also report an additional dynamic swarming phenotype that occurs over longer time periods.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the organism's size.

claim: Some strains of C. elegans aggregate into groups on food.
source: C. elegans collective behavior can contribute to bridging this scale gap. Some strains of this 1 mm-long roundworm are known to aggregate into groups on food (de Bono and Bargmann, 1998); here we also report an additional dynamic swarming phenotype that occurs over longer time periods.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: C. elegans crawls with negligible inertia.
source: C. elegans represents an intermediate scale not only in physical size but also in behavioral complexity—crawling with negligible inertia, limited to touch and chemical sensing, yet possessing a compact nervous system with 302 neurons (White et al., 1986) that supports a complex behavioral repertoire (Hart, 2006; Schwarz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the physical properties of C. elegans movement.

claim: C. elegans is limited to touch and chemical sensing.
source: C. elegans represents an intermediate scale not only in physical size but also in behavioral complexity—crawling with negligible inertia, limited to touch and chemical sensing, yet possessing a compact nervous system with 302 neurons (White et al., 1986) that supports a complex behavioral repertoire (Hart, 2006; Schwarz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans sensory capabilities.

claim: C. elegans possesses a compact nervous system with 302 neurons.
source: C. elegans represents an intermediate scale not only in physical size but also in behavioral complexity—crawling with negligible inertia, limited to touch and chemical sensing, yet possessing a compact nervous system with 302 neurons (White et al., 1986) that supports a complex behavioral repertoire (Hart, 2006; Schwarz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to White et al., 1986.

claim: Wild C. elegans form clusters on food at ambient oxygen concentrations.
source: Wild C. elegans form clusters on food at ambient oxygen concentrations, as do loss-of-function neuropeptide receptor 1 (npr-1) mutants.
evidence: This is a statement about wild-type behavior.

claim: Loss-of-function npr-1 mutants form clusters on food at ambient oxygen concentrations.
source: Wild C. elegans form clusters on food at ambient oxygen concentrations, as do loss-of-function neuropeptide receptor 1 (npr-1) mutants.
evidence: This is a statement about mutant behavior.

claim: The laboratory reference strain N2 has a gain-of-function mutation in the npr-1 gene that suppresses aggregation.
source: The laboratory reference strain N2, on the other hand, has a gain-of-function mutation in the npr-1 gene that suppresses aggregation (de Bono and Bargmann, 1998), rendering N2 animals solitary feeders.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to de Bono and Bargmann, 1998.

claim: N2 animals are solitary feeders.
source: The laboratory reference strain N2, on the other hand, has a gain-of-function mutation in the npr-1 gene that suppresses aggregation (de Bono and Bargmann, 1998), rendering N2 animals solitary feeders.
evidence: This is a consequence of the npr-1 mutation.

claim: A small genetic difference (two base pairs in one gene) has a big effect on the population-level behavioral phenotype in C. elegans.
source: Thus, a small genetic difference (just two base pairs in one gene for the npr-1(ad609lf) mutant) has a big effect on the population-level behavioral phenotype.
evidence: This is based on the comparison between npr-1 mutants and N2.

claim: Previous research on collective feeding has focused primarily on genetics and neural circuits rather than detailed understanding of the behavior itself.
source: Previous research on collective feeding has focused primarily on the genetics and neural circuits that govern aggregation (Bretscher et al., 2008; Busch et al., 2012; Chang et al., 2006; Cheung et al., 2005; de Bono et al., 2002; de Bono and Bargmann, 1998; Gray et al., 2004; Jang et al., 2017; Macosko et al., 2009), rather than on a detailed understanding of the behavior itself.
evidence: This is a characterization of the existing literature supported by multiple citations.

claim: Rogers et al. (2006) investigated behavioral motifs that might lead to cluster formation including direction reversals at the edge of clusters.
source: Rogers et al. (2006) is a notable exception and includes an investigation of the behavioral motifs that might lead to cluster formation including direction reversals at the edge of clusters.
evidence: This is a citation to previous work.

claim: It is not known whether the candidate motifs identified by Rogers et al. are sufficient to produce aggregation.
source: However, we do not know whether these candidate motifs are sufficient to produce aggregation.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: It is not known whether aggregation at short times and swarming at longer times are distinct behaviors or different emergent properties of the same underlying phenomenon.
source: We also do not know whether aggregation at short times and swarming at longer times are distinct behaviors or different emergent properties of the same underlying phenomenon.
evidence: This identifies a research question addressed by the study.

claim: Swarming refers to the collective movement of a coherent group of worms across a bacterial lawn.
source: Here, swarming refers to the collective movement of a coherent group of worms across a bacterial lawn (Figure 1A, Video 1).
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors with reference to figures.

claim: Swarming behavior in C. elegans occurs on a timescale of hours.
source: Here we report an additional dynamic swarming phenotype in aggregating C. elegans that occurs on a timescale of hours.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: N2 worms do not swarm under the experimental conditions used in this study.
source: Even though N2 worms do not swarm in our experiments (Figure 1B and C, N2 panels), they can swarm under appropriate conditions, such as when a clonal population has depleted almost all food (Hodgkin and Barnes, 1991) or on unpalatable Pseudomonas fluorescens bacterial lawns (personal communication from J. Hodgkin and G.M. Preston).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in figures.

claim: N2 worms can swarm when a clonal population has depleted almost all food.
source: Even though N2 worms do not swarm in our experiments (Figure 1B and C, N2 panels), they can swarm under appropriate conditions, such as when a clonal population has depleted almost all food (Hodgkin and Barnes, 1991) or on unpalatable Pseudomonas fluorescens bacterial lawns (personal communication from J. Hodgkin and G.M. Preston).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hodgkin and Barnes, 1991.

claim: N2 worms can swarm on unpalatable Pseudomonas fluorescens bacterial lawns.
source: Even though N2 worms do not swarm in our experiments (Figure 1B and C, N2 panels), they can swarm under appropriate conditions, such as when a clonal population has depleted almost all food (Hodgkin and Barnes, 1991) or on unpalatable Pseudomonas fluorescens bacterial lawns (personal communication from J. Hodgkin and G.M. Preston).
evidence: This is based on personal communication.

claim: Swarming in C. elegans does not require loss of npr-1 function in all environments.
source: Thus swarming in C. elegans does not require loss of npr-1 function in all environments.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that N2 can swarm under certain conditions.

claim: Forty npr-1 mutants form clusters that move on food over time.
source: Dynamic swarming occurs with just 40 npr-1 mutants (Figure 1B, top row), making it experimentally feasible to study.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in figures.

claim: A single npr-1 aggregate usually forms on the food patch and then moves around the lawn in a persistent but not necessarily directed manner.
source: Usually a single npr-1 aggregate forms on the food patch and then moves around the lawn in a persistent but not necessarily directed manner (Figure 1C, left; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), at a steady speed (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in figures.

claim: npr-1 clusters move at a steady speed.
source: Usually a single npr-1 aggregate forms on the food patch and then moves around the lawn in a persistent but not necessarily directed manner (Figure 1C, left; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), at a steady speed (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The onset of collective movement appears to coincide with local food depletion.
source: The onset of this collective movement appears to coincide with local food depletion, and continues until complete food depletion, at which time the cluster disperses.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: Collective movement continues until complete food depletion, at which time the cluster disperses.
source: The onset of this collective movement appears to coincide with local food depletion, and continues until complete food depletion, at which time the cluster disperses.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: More than one moving cluster may co-exist in npr-1 populations.
source: More than one moving cluster may co-exist, and occasionally a cluster may disperse and form elsewhere when it crosses its previous path (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), presumably due to local food depletion.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in figures.

claim: A cluster may disperse and form elsewhere when it crosses its previous path, presumably due to local food depletion.
source: More than one moving cluster may co-exist, and occasionally a cluster may disperse and form elsewhere when it crosses its previous path (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), presumably due to local food depletion.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations with a speculative explanation.

claim: The pattern of npr-1 cluster motion is reminiscent of a self-avoiding, persistent random walk.
source: The observed pattern of npr-1 cluster motion is reminiscent of a self-avoiding, persistent random walk (i.e. not returning to areas that the worms have previously been where there is no food left).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed movement patterns.

claim: After initially forming transient clusters on the lawn, N2 worms move radially outwards with no collective movement.
source: By contrast, after initially forming transient clusters on the lawn, N2 worms move radially outwards with no collective movement (Figure 1C, right).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in figures.

claim: Swarming may be a dynamic extension of the initial aggregation that occurs before food depletion.
source: Based on our observation that swarming appears to be driven by food depletion, we hypothesize the phenomenon may be a dynamic extension of the initial aggregation that occurs before depletion.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on observations.

claim: Fluorescence imaging with GFP-labeled pharynx minimizes overlap between animals, making it possible to track most individuals even when they are inside a dense cluster.
source: We therefore labeled the pharynx of worms with green fluorescent protein (GFP) and used fluorescence imaging in order to minimize overlap between animals (Video 2), making it possible to track most individuals even when they are inside a dense cluster (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology and its advantages.

claim: RFP-labeled worms allow both longer trajectories and full posture to be obtained in a subset of animals.
source: These RFP-labeled worms were recorded on a separate channel during simultaneous two-color imaging (Figure 2B), thus allowing both longer trajectories and the full posture to be obtained in a subset of animals.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: daf-22;npr-1 double mutants aggregate similarly to npr-1 single mutants.
source: daf-22(m130) mutants do not produce ascarosides, but daf-22;npr-1 double mutants aggregate similarly to npr-1 single mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with the observation that the hermaphrodite-attractive pheromone icas#3 is attractive to both N2 animals and npr-1 mutants (Srinivasan et al., 2012) and is thus unlikely to explain the difference in their propensity to aggregate.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The hermaphrodite-attractive pheromone icas#3 is attractive to both N2 animals and npr-1 mutants.
source: daf-22(m130) mutants do not produce ascarosides, but daf-22;npr-1 double mutants aggregate similarly to npr-1 single mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with the observation that the hermaphrodite-attractive pheromone icas#3 is attractive to both N2 animals and npr-1 mutants (Srinivasan et al., 2012) and is thus unlikely to explain the difference in their propensity to aggregate.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Srinivasan et al., 2012.

claim: Ascarosides are unlikely to explain the difference in aggregation propensity between N2 and npr-1 mutants.
source: daf-22(m130) mutants do not produce ascarosides, but daf-22;npr-1 double mutants aggregate similarly to npr-1 single mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with the observation that the hermaphrodite-attractive pheromone icas#3 is attractive to both N2 animals and npr-1 mutants (Srinivasan et al., 2012) and is thus unlikely to explain the difference in their propensity to aggregate.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results with daf-22 mutants.

claim: npr-1 mutants reverse more at increased neighbor densities, while N2 animals do not.
source: Calculating the reversal rates relative to that of worms at low densities, we found that npr-1 mutants reverse more at increased neighbor densities, while N2 animals do not (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both strains slow down when surrounded by many other worms, but the shift is more pronounced for npr-1 animals.
source: We found that both strains slow down when surrounded by many other worms, but the shift is more pronounced for npr-1 animals.
evidence: This is based on analysis of speed distributions at different densities.

claim: npr-1 worms move faster than N2 at low densities, showing a distinct peak at high speeds.
source: npr-1 worms move faster than N2 at low densities, showing a distinct peak at high speeds.
evidence: This is based on speed distribution data.

claim: As neighbor density increases, the high speed peak in npr-1 worms gradually becomes replaced by a peak at low speeds.
source: As neighbor density increases, this high speed peak gradually becomes replaced by a peak at low speeds, so that the overall speed distribution for npr-1 resembles that of N2 at very high densities.
evidence: This is based on speed distribution data at different densities.

claim: Worms are able to move inside of clusters.
source: We found that worms are able to move inside of clusters and observed that speed changes can occur prior to cluster entry and exit events (Figure 3D, Video 3 and Video 4).
evidence: This is based on tracking data of individual worms.

claim: Speed changes can occur prior to cluster entry and exit events.
source: We found that worms are able to move inside of clusters and observed that speed changes can occur prior to cluster entry and exit events (Figure 3D, Video 3 and Video 4).
evidence: This is based on tracking data shown in figures and videos.

claim: Speed change is neither purely mechanical nor a deterministic response to a certain neighbor density.
source: This change of speed is neither purely mechanical nor a deterministic response to a certain neighbor density, and suggests a mechanism in which worms probabilistically switch between different speeds.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that speed changes occur before entry/exit events.

claim: Worms probabilistically switch between different speeds.
source: This change of speed is neither purely mechanical nor a deterministic response to a certain neighbor density, and suggests a mechanism in which worms probabilistically switch between different speeds.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the observed data.

claim: npr-1 animals show quantifiably higher levels of aggregation than N2, especially at scales up to 1 mm (pair-correlation) and 2 mm (hierarchical clustering).
source: Using both measures, we found that as a population, npr-1 animals show quantifiably higher levels of aggregation than N2, especially at scales up to 1 mm (pair-correlation 'S1', Figure 4D) and 2 mm (hierarchical clustering 'S2', Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on spatial statistics calculated from tracking data.

claim: The positions of npr-1 worms are less spread-out and more heavy-tailed than those of N2.
source: This confirms that the positions of npr-1 worms are less spread-out and more heavy-tailed than those of N2 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on standard deviation and kurtosis statistics.

claim: The agent-based model can capture different aggregation phenotypes from solitary movement to aggregation by varying just two free parameters.
source: This demonstrates that our model can capture different aggregation phenotypes from solitary movement to aggregation (Figure 5E) by varying just two free parameters, and provides important general insights.
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in figures.

claim: Each behavior alone (just reversals or slowing) does not give the same level of aggregation as when both parameters are modulated.
source: Inspection of the model simulations shows that each behavior alone (just reversals or slowing) does not give the same level of aggregation as when both parameters are modulated (Figure 5E), so that using both behavioral components proves important.
evidence: This is based on comparison of simulation results.

claim: The model without taxis shows incomplete quantitative agreement with experimental data.
source: Quantifying the aggregation and comparing it to the npr-1 experiment, however, highlights incomplete quantitative agreement with both the pair correlation function and hierarchical clustering distribution (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is based on comparison between simulation and experimental data.

claim: The extended model with taxis shows markedly improved quantitative agreement with the experiments.
source: Results from our extended model (Figure 6A, Video 5 and Video 6) show markedly improved quantitative agreement with the experiments (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on comparison between simulation and experimental data.

claim: To achieve npr-1-like aggregation, the reversal and taxis parameters need to be higher than for N2.
source: In particular, to achieve npr-1-like aggregation, the reversal (r') and taxis (ft) parameters need to be higher than for N2, albeit not too high.
evidence: This is based on the posterior distributions from Bayesian inference.

claim: The density-dependence of the slowing rate is only subtly different between the two strains.
source: The density-dependence of the slowing rate (k's) is only subtly different between the two strains, while the dependence of the speeding up rate (k'f) is greater in npr-1, but with broader uncertainty.
evidence: This is based on the posterior distributions from Bayesian inference.

claim: Removing speed switching or taxis from the model disrupts aggregation.
source: These perturbed simulations show that removing speed switching or taxis from the model disrupts aggregation, while removing reversals reduces the overall quantitative agreement with experimental data (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, B–D).
evidence: This is based on simulation results with modified parameters.

claim: Removing reversals reduces the overall quantitative agreement with experimental data.
source: These perturbed simulations show that removing speed switching or taxis from the model disrupts aggregation, while removing reversals reduces the overall quantitative agreement with experimental data (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, B–D).
evidence: This is based on simulation results with modified parameters.

claim: All three behaviors (reversals, speed changes, and taxis) are necessary to quantitatively match aggregation in npr-1 mutants.
source: Thus, we conclude that we have identified sufficient behavioral components for aggregation, and that these are also necessary to quantitatively match aggregation in npr-1 mutants.
evidence: This is concluded from the perturbation simulations.

claim: The simulation with food depletion produced long-time dynamics qualitatively representative of the experimentally observed swarming.
source: Selecting the parameter combination best matching the npr-1 strain (Figure 6) and an appropriate food depletion rate (chosen such that all food was depleted no faster than observed in experiments), the resulting simulation produced long-time dynamics qualitatively representative of the experimentally observed swarming (Figure 7A–B, Video 7).
evidence: This is based on simulation results with food depletion.

claim: The model indicates that dynamic swarming of npr-1 aggregates may be explained as an emergent phenomenon resulting from individual locomotion.
source: Thus, the model indicates that dynamic swarming of npr-1 aggregates may be explained as an emergent phenomenon resulting from individual locomotion, and that the same behavioral mechanisms that produce the initial aggregates, when coupled with local food depletion, give rise to the observed swarming behavior.
evidence: This is concluded from the simulation results with food depletion.

claim: Aggregates break up when ambient O2 concentration is reduced to 7%.
source: Given that aggregates break up when ambient O2 concentration is reduced to 7% (Gray et al., 2004), the preferred concentration of npr-1 mutants, the most obvious candidate for the sensory cue guiding aggregation is O2 (Rogers et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gray et al., 2004.

claim: 7% O2 is the preferred concentration of npr-1 mutants.
source: Given that aggregates break up when ambient O2 concentration is reduced to 7% (Gray et al., 2004), the preferred concentration of npr-1 mutants, the most obvious candidate for the sensory cue guiding aggregation is O2 (Rogers et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Non-aggregating N2 worms prefer O2 concentrations lower than atmospheric (5–15%).
source: However, non-aggregating N2 worms also prefer O2 concentrations lower than atmospheric (5–15%) (Gray et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gray et al., 2004.

claim: A strong reduction of oxygen concentration inside an aggregate to near 7% is unlikely based on reaction-diffusion calculations.
source: Furthermore, a strong reduction of oxygen concentration inside an aggregate to near 7% is unlikely based on reaction-diffusion calculations: the diffusion of oxygen through worm tissue, or their oxygen consumption, would need to be several orders of magnitude different from estimated values to create O2 gradients as steep as reported by Rogers et al. (Appendix 2—figure 1).
evidence: This is based on calculations presented in the appendix.

claim: Worms have been reported to respond even to small changes in oxygen concentration.
source: However, as worms have been reported to respond even to small changes in oxygen concentration (McGrath et al., 2009), aggregation may still be mediated through a shallower local oxygen gradient.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McGrath et al., 2009.

claim: Spontaneous reversals have been implicated in bacterial aggregation at the microscale.
source: Indeed, key behavioral rules identified here for C. elegans aggregation have been observed at other scales. Spontaneous reversals have been implicated in bacterial aggregation at the microscale (Mercier and Mignot, 2016; Starruß et al., 2012; Thutupalli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Aggregating worms reverse mainly in response to leaving a cluster rather than spontaneously.
source: By contrast, aggregating worms reverse mainly in response to leaving a cluster rather than spontaneously, thus requiring more complex sensory processing and behavioral response than seen in bacterial systems.
evidence: This is based on the experimental observations and model results.

claim: Changes in movement speed are a common feature in motility-induced phase transitions.
source: Furthermore, changes in movement speed are a common feature in motility-induced phase transitions (Großmann et al., 2016; Redner et al., 2013b; Abaurrea Velasco et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Aggregation in C. elegans occurs at much lower numbers of objects (tens of worms) and lower densities (area fraction of 4–6%) than typically studied in active matter systems.
source: In contrast, aggregation in C. elegans occurs at much lower numbers of objects (tens of worms) and lower densities (area fraction of 4–6%) than typically studied in this field (thousands of objects at area fractions of 20–80%), and the density dependence of motility changes again emphasizes the role of more complex sensing and behavioral modulations common in macroscale animal groups such as fish shoals (Ward et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison between the current study and typical active matter studies.

claim: Collective behavior of C. elegans at the mesoscale draws from both ends of the size scale and complexity spectrum.
source: Thus, collective behavior of C. elegans at the mesoscale indeed draws from both ends of the size scale and complexity spectrum, linking the physical mechanisms familiar from microscopic cellular and active matter systems with the behavioral repertoire of larger multicellular organisms.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the findings in relation to other systems.

claim: Wild isolates of C. elegans aggregate to different degrees.
source: While hyper-social npr-1 mutants and hypo-social N2 worms show phenotypic extremes, wild isolates of C. elegans aggregate to different degrees (de Bono and Bargmann, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to de Bono and Bargmann, 1998.

claim: Even a very small increase in phenotypic dimensionality (from one to two) can reveal independent behavior-modifying loci.
source: Previous work has shown that even a very small increase in the phenotypic dimensionality (from one to two) can reveal independent behavior-modifying loci (Bendesky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bendesky et al., 2012.

claim: Inferring model parameters for data from multiple wild C. elegans strains would produce behavioral parameterizations that might serve as a powerful set of traits for finding further behavior-modifying loci.
source: Thus inferring model parameters for data from multiple wild C. elegans strains would produce behavioral parameterizations that might serve as a powerful set of traits for finding further behavior-modifying loci.
evidence: This is a proposed application of the modeling approach.

claim: Aggregation may serve to protect C. elegans from desiccation or UV radiation associated with the surface environment.
source: Aggregation may serve to protect C. elegans from desiccation or UV radiation associated with the surface environment (Busch and Olofsson, 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation.

claim: C. elegans swarming on unpalatable bacteria may facilitate predation through the collective action of secreted molecules that overcome bacterial defenses.
source: C. elegans swarming on unpalatable bacteria may also facilitate predation, perhaps through the collective action of secreted molecules that overcome bacterial defenses (personal communication from J. Hodgkin and G.M. Preston) in a manner similar to the well-described cooperative predation strategy used by Myxobacteria xanthus (Muñoz-Dorado et al., 2016; Pérez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on personal communication and citations.

claim: Aggregating strains are less fit in laboratory conditions.
source: The observation that aggregating strains are less fit in laboratory conditions (Andersen et al., 2014) suggested that social feeding is not an efficient strategy at least in abundant food conditions.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Andersen et al., 2014.

claim: The observed fitness difference between aggregating and non-aggregating strains is dissociable from the feeding strategy in the lab.
source: However, the observed fitness difference between aggregating and non-aggregating strains is actually dissociable from the feeding strategy in the lab (Zhao et al., 2018), leaving the question unresolved.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhao et al., 2018.

claim: In other systems, social feeding can increase fitness in natural environments via improved food detection and intake.
source: Furthermore, in other systems, social feeding can increase fitness in natural environments via improved food detection and intake (Cvikel et al., 2015; Li et al., 2014; Snijders et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work in other systems.

claim: 99.7 ± 0.4% of npr-1 worms are on food during the aggregation phase of the experiments.
source: Chemotaxis towards food can likely be ignored as our experiments were performed on thin, even bacterial lawns, and worms are mostly on food during the aggregation phase of the experiments (99.7 ± 0.4% for npr-1 and 99.8 ± 0.3% for N2, mean ±S.D.).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements.

claim: 99.8 ± 0.3% of N2 worms are on food during the aggregation phase of the experiments.
source: Chemotaxis towards food can likely be ignored as our experiments were performed on thin, even bacterial lawns, and worms are mostly on food during the aggregation phase of the experiments (99.7 ± 0.4% for npr-1 and 99.8 ± 0.3% for N2, mean ±S.D.).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements.

claim: Ascarosides are important for processes such as mating and dauer formation in C. elegans.
source: Although ascarosides are important for processes such as mating and dauer formation in C. elegans (Srinivasan et al., 2008), it is less clear whether long-range signaling via pheromones plays a role in aggregation (de Bono et al., 2002; Macosko et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Srinivasan et al., 2008.

claim: It is less clear whether long-range signaling via pheromones plays a role in aggregation.
source: Although ascarosides are important for processes such as mating and dauer formation in C. elegans (Srinivasan et al., 2008), it is less clear whether long-range signaling via pheromones plays a role in aggregation (de Bono et al., 2002; Macosko et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about uncertainty in the field, supported by citations.

claim: daf-22(m130) mutants do not produce ascarosides.
source: daf-22(m130) mutants do not produce ascarosides, but daf-22;npr-1 double mutants aggregate similarly to npr-1 single mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with the observation that the hermaphrodite-attractive pheromone icas#3 is attractive to both N2 animals and npr-1 mutants (Srinivasan et al., 2012) and is thus unlikely to explain the difference in their propensity to aggregate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the daf-22 mutation.

claim: Principal component analysis of lone versus in-cluster npr-1 worms revealed similar amplitudes in the posture modes.
source: While postural changes do not seem to be a main driver of aggregation as principal component analysis of lone versus in-cluster npr-1 worms revealed similar amplitudes in the posture modes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), we found experimental evidence for density-dependence of both reversal rates and speed and that these differ between the two strains we studied.
evidence: This is based on data analysis shown in figures.

claim: Postural changes do not seem to be a main driver of aggregation.
source: While postural changes do not seem to be a main driver of aggregation as principal component analysis of lone versus in-cluster npr-1 worms revealed similar amplitudes in the posture modes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), we found experimental evidence for density-dependence of both reversal rates and speed and that these differ between the two strains we studied.
evidence: This is inferred from the PCA analysis.

claim: The median experimental cluster speed is 172 μm/min.
source: Tracking the centroid of worms in our simulations, we find a comparable cluster speed as the median experimental value of 172 μm/min (Figure 1D) for a range of feeding rates (Figure 7C) (feeding rate is an unknown parameter as our model only accounts for relative food concentration).
evidence: This value is stated in the text and referenced to Figure 1D.

claim: One-hour fluorescence recordings of npr-1 animals consist of reproducible temporal dynamics encompassing three phases: transient, aggregation, and swarming.
source: One-hour fluorescence recordings of npr-1 animals under our experimental conditions consist of reproducible temporal dynamics encompassing three phases: transient (animals move about the lawn and start to form clusters), aggregation (clusters largely remain stable with individuals entering and exiting), and swarming (worms move across the lawn in persistent clusters) (see sample Video 2).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Percentage of in-cluster worms remain largely consistent throughout the aggregation and swarming phases.
source: Percentage of in-cluster worms remain largely consistent throughout the latter two phases, except that clusters remain in place during the aggregation phase and become dynamic during the swarming phase.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The correlation between worm velocity and the vector towards nearby worms is nearly zero in both experiments and simulations for all distances up to 2 mm.
source: Searching for evidence of taxis in the experimental tracking data, we calculated the correlation between worm velocity and the vector towards nearby worms, and found this correlation to be nearly zero in both experiments and simulations for all distances up to 2 mm (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B1–2), which is larger than the size of a typical worm cluster.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of tracking data.

claim: A taxis behavior similar to the simulations may be present in experiments, even if it is difficult to detect with correlation analysis.
source: Thus, our analysis shows that a taxis behavior similar to our simulations may be present in experiments, even if it is difficult to detect with correlation analysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the limitations of the tracking methodology.

claim: The reversal rate shows a similar increase with density that is greater for npr-1 than N2.
source: We compared the other inferred parameters with experimental measurements: The reversal rate shows a similar increase with density that is greater for npr-1 than N2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is based on comparison between model and experimental data.

claim: Aggregation in the model is not sensitive to speed switching rates.
source: However, aggregation in the model is not sensitive to speed switching rates, as shown by the broad posterior distributions for the inferred parameters (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This is inferred from the posterior distributions.
